title: The foolish seedling
teaches: Gibberellin, the hormone that lengthens stems, found through a rice disease, and the short wheat and rice of the Green Revolution

blocks.text: Rice farmers in Japan had a name for a disease that made no sense. In a paddy of young rice, a few seedlings would shoot up far taller than their neighbours, spindly and pale yellow-green. For a week or two they looked like the best plants in the field. Then they fell over, or set little or no grain, and many died. Farmers called it *bakanae*, the foolish seedling disease. In bad years it cost a fifth or more of the crop in some districts.

In 1898 the plant pathologist Shotaro Hori showed that the sick seedlings were infected with a fungus. That much was ordinary: plenty of fungi make plants sick. What was strange was the symptom. A fungus that is eating a plant should stunt it. This one made its victims grow taller and faster than healthy plants, as if it had found the plant's own accelerator and pressed it down.

In 1926 Eiichi Kurosawa, working in Taiwan, which was then ruled by Japan, grew the fungus in a flask of nutrient broth, then filtered out every scrap of fungus. When he put the clear liquid on healthy rice seedlings, they shot up and went pale exactly as infected ones did. The fungus was not doing it by its presence. It was making a chemical, and the chemical was enough.

In 1935 Teijiro Yabuta at Tokyo purified the substance and named it **gibberellin**, after the fungus, *Gibberella*. Japanese work on it went on through the 1930s, published in Japanese, and the rest of the world mostly missed it until after the Second World War. In the 1950s chemists in Britain and the United States produced it in quantity and sprayed it on every plant they could think of. Dwarf plants of many kinds shot up to normal height. Then, in 1958, Jake MacMillan found gibberellins in the seeds of runner beans. The fungus had not invented the molecule. It was making a plant hormone, one that plants use themselves to lengthen their stems, and pouring an overdose into the rice.[^why]

Gibberellins make stems grow longer between their leaves, mainly by letting cells stretch further and partly by making them divide more. They also wake many seeds: a germinating barley grain makes gibberellin, which tells it to start digesting its starch store into sugar; maltsters add gibberellin to sprouting barley to make the malt for beer faster. Of the hundred or so gibberellins since found in plants and fungi, only a few are active; the rest are steps on the way to making them or breaking them down.

parts.title: Making the signal, or hearing it

blocks.text: Mendel's short peas, which the branch on crops and breeding takes up, were short because of a single gene. It is tempting to read that as a gene for height, as if somewhere in the pea's DNA there were a line that says how tall to grow. In 1997 the gene was found. It codes for an enzyme that does the last step in making active gibberellin. Mendel's short pea has a version of the enzyme that works poorly, so the plant makes too little of the hormone, and its stems stay short.

blocks.caption: A tall pea, Mendel's short pea and a semi-dwarf wheat, before and after spraying with gibberellin.

blocks.text: Spray that pea with gibberellin and it grows tall. Spray the short wheat of the Green Revolution and nothing happens. Its dwarfing genes don't touch the hormone. They change a protein inside the cells that normally holds growth back until gibberellin arrives and removes it. In the dwarf wheat the brake can't be removed. The plant makes plenty of gibberellin, but its cells ignore it, and it stays short. Two ways to be a dwarf: make too little of the signal, or be deaf to it.

Either way the gene does not set the height. It makes a part, an enzyme or a brake, in a chain of steps that ends in cells growing, and height comes out of the whole chain, along with light, water and food.

After the Second World War, factories built to make nitrogen for explosives turned to fertiliser (lesson 10), and it became cheap enough to spread by the hundredweight. More nitrogen gives bigger, heavier heads of grain. But it also gives taller, softer straw, and a tall stalk with a heavy head on top is a long lever. In a summer storm, with wet heads and wind, the stalks bend at the base and the crop lies flat. This is **lodging**. Grain lying on wet ground sprouts or rots, and harvesting machines can't pick it up. With the old tall wheats, more fertiliser past a point gave less grain, not more, as the figure shows.

blocks.caption: A field of tall wheat and a field of semi-dwarf wheat given more and more nitrogen fertiliser, and a summer storm. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a fertiliser level where the tall wheat falls and the semi-dwarf stands

blocks.text: The answer came from Japan too. In 1935 the breeder Gonjiro Inazuka released a wheat called Norin 10, with stiff stalks about two feet high, bred from an old Japanese dwarf variety called Daruma crossed with two American wheats. After the war an American agricultural adviser in occupied Japan, Cecil Salmon, sent seed home. At the state college in Pullman, now Washington State University, Orville Vogel spent years crossing Norin 10 into wheats suited to eastern Washington, and in 1961 released Gaines, a semi-dwarf winter wheat that set yield records on the Palouse, the rolling wheat country around Pullman (the crops branch has a lesson on it).

Vogel also sent seed of his crosses to Norman Borlaug in Mexico, who bred them into Mexican wheats. Those semi-dwarfs went to India and Pakistan in the mid-1960s, where, grown with fertiliser and irrigation, they helped India's wheat harvest more than double between 1965 and 1972. The same thing was done for rice at the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines with a dwarf from Taiwan, giving IR8 in 1966. Borlaug was given the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.[^revolution] The new varieties did not only stand up. A plant builds its straw out of the sugar its leaves make, and a short plant spends less of its sugar on straw and more on grain: the grain's share of a wheat plant's dry weight rose from about a third to nearly a half.

Gibberellin and auxin are not the only plant hormones, and one of the others is a gas. In the nineteenth century, city trees near leaking gas mains dropped their leaves, and in greenhouses lit by gas lamps, plants grew stunted and twisted. In 1901 a Russian student, Dimitry Neljubow, found the culprit in the lighting gas: **ethylene**, a small molecule of two carbons and four hydrogens. Then it turned out that plants make it themselves.

Ripening fruit gives off ethylene, and ethylene makes fruit ripen, so ripening spreads: one ripe apple in a barrel speeds up the rest. Growers use it. Bananas are shipped green and hard, then ripened in sealed rooms with a little ethylene added. At home, a green tomato or a hard avocado shut in a paper bag with a ripe banana softens a day or two sooner, because the banana's ethylene builds up in the bag. Ethylene also tells leaves and fruit when to drop, and makes a seedling pushing up through soil stay short and thick and keep its tip hooked over.

A plant's hormones work together. Auxin, gibberellin, ethylene and a few others each push growth one way or another, and what a cell does depends on the mix it receives and on which receptors it has. Lesson 15 adds the plant's way of reading light and time, which sets many of those hormones going.

blocks.caption: Six questions on gibberellin and short crops
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why did rice infected with the bakanae fungus grow so tall?
choices: The fungus makes gibberellin, a plant growth hormone
The fungus fed the rice extra sugar
The rice was stretching to escape the fungus
items.why: Kurosawa showed the fungus's filtered broth alone did it. The chemical, gibberellin, turned out to be a hormone plants make themselves to lengthen their stems.

items.ask: Mendel's short pea is sprayed with gibberellin. What happens, and why?
choices: It grows tall, because it was only short of the hormone
Nothing, because its cells can't respond
It dies, because the dose is too much
items.why: Its gene makes a weak enzyme for the last step in making gibberellin. Supply the hormone and it grows normally.

items.ask: Semi-dwarf wheat from Norin 10 is sprayed with gibberellin. What happens?
choices: Nothing: its cells can't act on the hormone
It grows tall, like the pea
items.why: Its dwarfing genes change a protein that holds growth back until gibberellin removes it. In the dwarf the brake can't be removed.

choices: Tall stalks with heavy heads bending over and lying flat
Grain sprouting in the ear before harvest
items.why: Fertiliser gives heavy heads and tall soft straw. In wind and rain the stalks fall, and the grain rots or can't be harvested.

items.ask: Why could farmers give semi-dwarf wheat much more fertiliser than the old tall wheats?
choices: Its short stiff straw holds the heavier heads up in a storm
Its roots take up fertiliser more slowly
It can make its own nitrogen from the air
items.why: Fertiliser makes heavy heads. On tall straw they fall over and the grain is lost; short straw keeps them standing, so more fertiliser keeps giving more grain.

items.ask: A green tomato is shut in a paper bag with a ripe banana. Why does it ripen sooner?
choices: The banana gives off ethylene gas, which sets ripening going
The banana's sugar seeps into it
items.why: Ripening fruit releases ethylene, a plant hormone that makes other fruit ripen. In a bag it builds up.

summary: **Bakanae seedlings shot up, went pale and fell over.** The rice was infected by a fungus.
**The fungus makes gibberellin.** Kurosawa's filtered broth (1926) did it alone; plants make the same hormone to lengthen stems.
**There are two ways to be a dwarf.** Make too little gibberellin (Mendel's pea, Green Revolution rice) or be unable to respond (Norin 10 wheat).
**A gene makes a part, not a height.** Height comes from a chain of steps that a gene's enzyme or protein takes part in.
**Tall wheat given lots of fertiliser lodges.** Heavy heads on long straw fall flat in a storm.
**Semi-dwarfs stand up and put more into grain.** Vogel's Gaines (1961) and Borlaug's wheats helped India's wheat harvest more than double in seven years.
**Ethylene is a gas that ripens fruit.** One ripe fruit speeds up the ones around it.

why.title: Why would a fungus do that?
why.text: Making its host grow tall and weak seems to help the fungus. Gibberellin is known to damp down some of a plant's defences against infection, which may be what the fungus gains. The fungus spreads from rice that falls over and rots in the paddy, and from infected seed.

revolution.title: The Green Revolution's costs
revolution.text: The new varieties needed fertiliser, irrigation and pesticides, which richer farmers could buy more easily, and they replaced many local varieties. The water table in much of the Indian Punjab has been falling by tens of centimetres a year. Historians still argue over how the gains and costs were shared, but the extra grain fed hundreds of millions of people.
